plain_text:
Conservation Commission 
Meeting Minutes 
July 13th, 2026 
City Hall – Levi Lincoln Chamber,  
with remote participation options available via Zoom online at 
https://worcesterma.zoomgov.com/j/1604682366 and  
call-in number 1-669-254-5252 (Meeting ID: 160 468 2366). 
 
Attendance: 
Commissioners 
Present: 
 
 
 
Staff Present: 
Diane Fratoni, Chair 
Devin Canton, Vice Chair 
Lindsay Nystrom, Commissioner 
Stuart Kirshner, Commissioner 
 
Eric Flint, Division of Planning & Regulatory Services (DPRS) 
Mattie VandenBoom, Division of Planning & Regulatory Services 
(DPRS)  
Call to Order 
Chair Fratoni called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 PM. 
Requests for Continuances, Postponements and Withdrawals 
Item 3 – 497 Granite Street – Notice of Intent (CC-2026-026 & DEP# 349-1452) 
Request to postpone the public hearing to 08/03/2026 & extend the constructive grant deadline 
to 08/25/2026 
Mr. Flint read the requests for postponements into the record.  
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted by roll call vote 4-0 to postpone the public hearings as discussed.  
New Business – Request for Determination of Applicability 
1) Providence and Worcester Railroad Right-of-Way - CC-2026-033 
There was no representative present at the meeting for this item.
2) 166 Moreland Street (MBL 25-045-011-2) – CC-2026-038 
Rich Kirby, LEC Environmental, on behalf of the applicant, Edrrysa and Jesula Jean, 
reviewed the proposed project.  The project entails installation of a 16‑by‑32‑foot 
above‑ground pool and a 10‑by‑16‑foot deck on the west side of the pool. Mr. Kirby 
explained that contractors would shave down elevated portions of the west side to create a 
level pad and push that material eastward to fill the lower area, thereby establishing a flat 
surface while avoiding any impact on the resource areas. Straw wattles would be installed 
along the downgradient edge to contain sediment during the brief grading operation.  
 
The owners also proposed extending an existing polyvinyl fence to fully enclose the yard, 
connecting it to existing fencing near the garage. The proposal included removal of one 
hazard tree located near the property boundary. Mr. Kirby noted that the tree was 
smothered by Asiatic bittersweet vines and exhibited significant decline.   
 
Mr. Kirby then described a previous 2020 enforcement order on the property relating to 
vegetation removal in the eastern portion of the yard. Restoration was conducted in 
accordance with the Commission’s directives, including installation of several saplings and 
shrubs. Although only eight of twelve marked shrubs could be located due to dense natural 
regrowth, he explained that the area had become heavily vegetated with native species, 
effectively fulfilling the functional objectives of the restoration plan. The applicant 
submitted a restoration monitoring report, confirming that the area had been successfully 
vegetated.   
 
Ms. VandenBoom confirmed that because the proposed pool and deck were located over 
fifty feet from the wetland, the project constituted a minor activity exempt from filing 
under the Wetlands Protection Act (WPA), though filing was required under the local 
Wetlands Ordinance. She reported that the fence extension would not increase impacts 
because it would be located farther away from the wetland than the current fence. 
Regarding the tree removal, staff noted that photographs showed the tree was in poor 
health and that bittersweet infestation contributed to its decline; therefore, staff had no 
objection to its removal. 
 
Ms. VandenBoom also reported that the applicant had satisfied the conditions of the prior 
enforcement order, and restoration work completed the previous year had been successful. 
Based on monitoring reports demonstrating healthy regrowth and adequate native 
vegetation, staff recommended that the Commission lift the enforcement order.  
 
Ms. VandenBoom recommended a condition requiring that any dewatering of the pool be 
directed away from the resource area to avoid erosion or migration of chemically treated 
water.  
Commissioners engaged in a lengthy, detailed discussion concerning the appropriate 
standards for pool water discharge. Questions were raised regarding access for 
construction equipment, with Mr. Kirby confirming that smaller equipment would be 
sufficient to navigate the tight yard space without causing additional disturbance.
The bulk of the discussion concerned chlorine levels, pH thresholds, and methods to 
ensure safe discharge of water during seasonal pool draining. Several Commissioners 
raised concerns about potential impacts on the wetland should inadequately treated pool 
water be discharged, noting that the site slopes uniformly toward the wetland. Mr. Kirby 
advised that chlorine dissipates naturally when untreated for several days and that 
commonly available home test strips could reliably indicate chlorine concentrations. 
Mr. Kirby researched thresholds during the meeting and cited guidance from the City of 
Edgerton, Kansas, which identifies 0.1 parts per million (ppm) as the maximum chlorine 
level compatible with discharge to vegetated areas. Additional discussion addressed pH, 
with Chair Fratoni referencing a Massachusetts DCR document stating that water should 
have a pH between 6.5 and 8.5 before discharge. The applicant confirmed that these values 
were typical for pool operations and that test strips measuring both pH and chlorine were 
readily available.    
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted by roll call vote 4-0 by to issue a negative determination of 
applicability as discussed.    
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 by roll call vote to lift the Enforcement Order.    
List of Exhibits:  
Exhibit A: Request for Determination of Applicability; dated 06/24/2026; prepared 
by Rich Kirby, LEC Environmental   
New Business – Notice of Intent 
3) 2 Northboro Street (MBL 17-025-04+05) – CC-2026-041 
Michael Andrade, Graves Engineering, Inc., on behalf of REMP Realty, LLC, the applicant, 
comprehensive description of the property and project proposal.  The subject parcel is 
situated at the corner of Northboro, Peabody, and Plantation Streets, consisting of roughly 
one-quarter acre of land containing an existing one‑story building. He explained the 
history of the property, noting that it previously served as a satellite dry cleaning 
establishment. The building has been vacant for a considerable period.  
The proposed project intends to renovate and expand the structure into a two‑story 
building and modernize the entire site. Improvements include reconfigured curb cuts, new 
parking layouts, updated lighting, landscaping, and fully redesigned stormwater 
management systems. The renovated building and site will house “Napoli Deli,” a business 
currently operating in Shrewsbury and seeking relocation to the family‑owned property in 
Worcester.  
Mr. Andrade stated that the Zoning Board of Appeals had already granted necessary 
approvals and that Planning Board review was scheduled for later that week. He 
emphasized that the Conservation Commission’s review was triggered not by the presence 
of wetlands—none exist on the parcel—but because the site lies within the local stormwater 
protection zone and within 100 feet of a catch basin on Peabody Street.
Ms. VandenBoom reviewed staff comments. She noted that staff had reviewed the 
stormwater management system in detail and had questioned the applicant about the 
presence of ledge on the site. A response letter was issued by the representative, explaining 
that the stormwater system had been designed with full knowledge of the subsurface 
conditions and would still meet recharge requirements. She indicated that staff concerns 
had been addressed.   
Chair Fratoni asked about the existing and proposed grades on site. Mr. Andrade 
explained that the site was not flat, with the highest point located in the southeastern 
corner. The land slopes downward toward both Peabody Street and Northboro Street. The 
existing parking area along Northboro Street is relatively level, but grading elsewhere must 
be adjusted slightly to accommodate the proposed improvements.  
Chair Fratoni inquired about stormwater flow under current and proposed conditions.  
Mr. Andrade illustrated the drainage patterns and the stormwater collection system, 
noting that runoff will enter either of two catch basins that lead to treatment units and 
then to underground infiltration structures before discharge. He also highlighted the need 
for a retaining wall and confirmed that the grading plan had been prepared to minimize 
ledge removal. 
No comments from the public.   
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 by roll call vote to close the public hearing.    
In addition to the standard conditions, Ms. VandenBoom recommended revised plans, 
infiltration unit inspection, certification of stormwater infrastructure, dust control, 
dewatering, cement truck washing, spill prevention and ongoing condition for stormwater 
management system maintenance, and sand/salt.         
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 by roll call vote to issue the Order of Conditions as discussed.    
List of Exhibits:  
Exhibit A: Notice of Intent; dated 05/27/2026; prepared by Michael Andrade, 
Graves Engineering, Inc. 
Exhibit B: Site Plan; dated 05/19/2026; prepared by Michael Andrade, Graves 
Engineering, Inc.  
Exhibit C: Stormwater Report; dated 01/19/2026; prepared by Michael Andrade, 
Graves Engineering, Inc. 
Exhibit D: Division of Planning and Regulatory Comments; dated 06/12/2026; 
prepared by Eric Flint and Mattie VandenBoom 
Exhibit E:  Response to Comments; dated 06/12/2026; prepared by Michael 
Andrade, Graves Engineering, Inc.
5) 283 Lake Avenue (Quinsigamond State Park) (MBL 41-047-00004)  
Andrea Kendall, LEC Environmental Consultants, Inc. and Andrew Keel, Hatch Design 
Consultants, provided an extensive overview of the improvement project at Lake 
Quinsigamond State Park on behalf of the applicant, Department of Conservation and 
Recreation (DCR).   
Mr. Keel explained that it is part of a larger two‑phase initiative to redesign a portion of 
Lake Quinsigamond State Park. The existing waterfront includes an inaccessible 
swimming beach that DCR seeks to permanently close due to safety and accessibility 
constraints. Phase 1 of the improvement project focuses on the area immediately 
surrounding the bath house and a portion of the existing lower parking lot. The plan 
proposes transforming that asphalt area into a spray deck, playground, and universally 
accessible recreational space.  
Ms. Kendall then described the resource areas near the project site. She explained that an 
intermittent stream flows from an adjacent city property and meanders through the 
project area before broadening into a vegetated wetland system. The water then leaves the 
wetland via a raised culvert structure and enters Lake Quinsigamond through an 
underground pipe. She identified the Bank of the intermittent stream, Bordering 
Vegetated Wetland (BVW), and the 100‑foot buffer zone, portions of which overlap with 
the limits of the proposed work. She noted that there is no mapped floodplain associated 
with the site.      
Ms. Kendall described vegetation within the project area, noting a mix of native and 
non‑native species, including a notable presence of Norway Maple and invasive understory 
species such as burning bush and bittersweet. The applicant is proposing removal of nine 
trees along the upper slope—eight of which are non‑native Norway maple—as well as 
removal of invasive vegetation. She explained that the project would restore the area by 
planting twenty‑six native trees and placing a woodland seed mix along portions of the 
slope to improve habitat diversity and restore ecological function. 
Hillary Homes, Hatch Design Consultants, reviewed the proposed grading and drainage 
improvements.  She explained that the current parking lot lacks any infiltration or 
significant stormwater treatment and that the existing outfall requires repair and 
replacement to meet contemporary design standards.  She detailed the proposed 
stormwater system, which includes deep‑sump catch basins, area drains, and an 
underground infiltration gallery composed of perforated pipe surrounded by crushed 
stone. She emphasized that this project falls within a DCR priority watershed and must 
therefore maximize pollution reduction, especially in relation to phosphorus.  She did note 
that test pits had not been conducted yet but will be conducted prior to construction.
Mr. Flint reported that staff had visited the site with the project team and found the 
proposal beneficial in many respects. The project substantially reduces impervious surface 
area, improves stormwater treatment, removes invasive vegetation, and restores native 
habitat.  He stated that staff had no concerns regarding the proposed scope. Because the 
Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) had not yet issued a file number, the 
Commission cannot close the hearing or issue an Order of Conditions at this meeting. Mr. 
Flint also stated that staff were comfortable conditioning the infiltration test pits to occur 
later during the permitting process. 
Chair Fratoni raised questions about the spray deck’s water supply and drainage. Mr. Keel 
confirmed that the spray deck uses potable city water, not re‑circulated water, and that all 
spray deck drainage would flow into the infiltration system.   
Due to the absence of a DEP file number, the Chair Fratoni entertained a motion to 
continue the hearing until August 3. 
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 by roll call vote to continue the public hearing to August 3rd, 2026.    
List of Exhibits:  
Exhibit A: Notice of Intent; dated 06/22/2026; prepared by Andrea Kendall  
Exhibit B: Site Plan; dated 04/2026; prepared by Hilary A. Holmes, Hatch Design 
Consultants  
Exhibit C: Stormwater Report; dated 06/10/2026; prepared by Hilary A. Holmes, 
Hatch Design Consultants    
 
6) 35 State Road (MBL 32-019-00316) - CC-2026-045 & DEP#349- 14xx 
Paul Lenkarski, the applicant, reviewed the proposal involving complete removal of the 
current structure and construction of a new residential building containing eight 
one‑bedroom units. The redevelopment will include creation of sixteen parking spaces, 
which complies with Worcester’s zoning requirements for a development of this size. He 
noted that approximately fourteen parking spaces currently exist on the site.  He noted 
that the redevelopment will include installation of an underground stormwater retention 
area designed to manage runoff from both the parking lot and the building’s roof drains. 
He added that accessory landscaping and related site improvements were also planned as 
part of the complete redevelopment of the parcel. 
Mr. Flint began by noting that the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) had not 
yet issued a file number for this Notice of Intent. Therefore, the Commission could not 
close the hearing or vote on the matter that evening.  He then provided detailed comments 
concerning the wetland resource areas associated with the project.
Mr. Flint explained that a bordering vegetated wetland (BVW) is located to the east of the 
property and that a stream flows near or through this portion of the site. The wetland line 
was depicted clearly on the submitted plans, and staff had visited the site to review the 
delineation. He reported that staff had no concerns with the accuracy of the flagging, 
although many of the flags had faded; new flags bearing legible identification numbers 
would be required so that staff and the Commission could verify locations during any 
future field visits.   
Mr. Flint stated that stormwater considerations were particularly complex due to the site’s 
location within Zone A of a public drinking water supply. Under the Massachusetts 
Stormwater Standards, specifically Standard 6, new discharges within Zone A are 
prohibited except for projects associated directly with public drinking water infrastructure. 
Staff explained that MassDEP maps Zone A differently from the watershed protection 
zones shown under DCR’s jurisdiction and that, in this instance, the site fell within 
MassDEP’s Zone A, even though it was not located within DCR’s primary or secondary 
protection zones. He acknowledged that such mapping discrepancies were uncommon but 
nevertheless controlling under the state’s stormwater standards.  Because of the regulatory 
complexity, staff reported that they had initiated an inquiry with MassDEP seeking 
clarification. Specifically, staff asked whether, under the “maximum extent practicable” 
framework, MassDEP might allow a new discharge within Zone A if the alternative—sheet 
flow across the site—would be less protective of water quality.  
Mr. Flint added that a small number of additional revisions would be needed, including 
updates to erosion‑control details and potential installation of native buffer plantings 
between the parking lot and the wetland to enhance natural filtration. Staff also informed 
the Commission that the Commonwealth’s watershed protection program had notified the 
City that the project would require a variance under the Watershed Protection Act. Staff 
had discussed the matter with representatives from the program, and although no major 
concerns were raised, both sides agreed to maintain communication as reviews 
progressed.  
Finally, Mr. Flint indicated that, regardless of whether MassDEP ultimately allows a 
discharge in Zone A, modifications to the applicant’s stormwater report would likely be 
necessary to address Standard 6 explicitly and to ensure that any discharge or infiltration 
method complies with state requirements. 
Chair Fratoni asked whether the applicant understood the regulatory complexities and the 
significance of the property’s location within a drinking water protection zone. Mr. 
Lenkarski responded that he and his engineer were aware of the issue, noting that they had 
already met with DCR and applied for the necessary variance. He explained that under 
DCR’s mapping, the property lies within a “low‑yield zone,” rather than the more 
restrictive 200‑foot or 400‑foot protection zones. However, Mr. Flint clarified that 
MassDEP’s mapping governs Standard 6 compliance, not DCR’s mapping under the 
Watershed Protection Act.              
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 by roll call vote to continue the public hearing to August 3rd, 2026.
List of Exhibits:  
Exhibit A: Notice of Intent; dated 06/22/2026; prepared by Vito Colonna, 
Connorstone Engineering, Inc.    
Exhibit B: Site Plan; dated 05/21/2026; revised 06/22/2026; prepared by Vito 
Colonna, Connorstone Engineering, Inc. 
Exhibit C: Stormwater Report; dated 05/20/2026; prepared by Vito Colonna, 
Connorstone Engineering, Inc.  
Exhibit D: Wetland Report; dated 10/24/2025; Doug Dillon, Goddard Consulting   
 
New Business – Request Amended Order of Conditions  
7) Lots 9, 10, 11, & 12 Chester Street (MBL 55-004-001C9, -01C10, -01C11, & -
01C12) - CC-2026-043 (CC-2025-053 & DEP#349-1428 
James Tetreault of Expedited Engineering appeared on behalf of the applicant, Modern 
Structures, Inc., whose principal, Mike Fam, was also present. Mr. Tetreault explained that 
the Commission originally issued an Order of Conditions in October of the previous year 
for the construction of four single‑family homes on these lots. During subsequent Planning 
Board review, as well as review by the City’s newly appointed Director of Engineering, 
several issues were identified that required modifications to the approved grading plan.  
Mr. Tetreault stated that the new Director of Engineering had requested a geotechnical 
analysis of the hillside behind the proposed homes to determine slope stability. A 
geotechnical engineer conducted soil borings and evaluated stability in accordance with 
standard slope failure models. The analysis concluded that the slope would need to be 
graded to at least 2.66:1 to meet acceptable factors of safety. In response, the applicant 
redesigned the slopes to grade them at 2.8:1, slightly flatter than required. To 
accommodate the required slope, backyard depths were reduced on several lots. The 
applicant also prepared new stamped plans for a retaining wall located on Lot 9. 
Mr. Flint stated that the primary wetland concern is related to the increased clearing 
necessary to implement the flatter slope design. He noted that the situation was somewhat 
unique because the wetland is located upgradient of the work area rather than 
downgradient. As a result, erosion concerns pertain primarily to runoff washing toward 
Chester Street rather than toward the wetland. Mr. Flint expressed no objection to the 
revised slope grading but recommended that the Commission consider requiring 
additional native plantings on the hillside to compensate for loss of tree canopy and to 
increase slope stabilization through long-rooted vegetation.   
Chair Fratoni expressed concerns with runoff to the street during construction and clear 
cutting of the hillside.  Mr. Tetreault explained how construction would proceed in phases 
to minimize erosion. For example, although trees would be cut early in the project, stumps 
would remain in place until grading occurred, thereby reducing soil disturbance. 
Temporary sediment basins would be created at strategic locations during each phase, 
eventually consolidating into a single basin at Lot 12 as construction progressed. A 
designated stockpile area and construction entrance were included in the plans.
Chair Fratoni questioned how trucks and construction equipment would access the site 
without destabilizing newly graded slopes. Mr. Tetreault stated that the initial access point 
would be located at Lot 12 and that equipment movements would be confined to 
designated work zones shown on the interim plans.  
Chair Fratoni also inquired about seasonal stabilization. Mr. Tetreault explained that if 
some slopes could not be seeded due to winter conditions, the applicant would stabilize 
those areas with stump grindings—material preferred for its ability to adhere to soil and 
provide erosion resistance during freeze‑thaw cycles.  
Mr. Flint asked about the seed mix being used on the slope. Mr. Tetreault confirmed that a 
slope stabilization mix containing fescue, rye, and related species was included on the 
landscape sheet.  However, upon further discussion, Commissioners and staff agreed that 
the hillside should be seeded with a conservation or no‑mow native erosion control mix 
rather than a conventional lawn mix. The Commission emphasized that a native, unmowed 
mix would provide a stronger root systems for slope stability, allow natural succession of 
native species, and reduce long‑term maintenance burdens.  
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 by roll call vote to close the public hearing.    
Mr. Flint recommended Replacing the prior plan reference with the May 26, 2026 revised 
plans; requiring the hillside to be seeded with a native, no‑mow conservation erosion 
control mix; retaining the condition requiring submission of an Operation & Maintenance 
plan for the area drains; removing the outdated condition relating to infiltration trenches, 
which were removed from the revised design.         
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 by roll call vote to issue the Order of Conditions as discussed. 
List of Exhibits:  
Exhibit A: Request for Amended Order of Conditions; dated 06/11/2026; prepared 
by James Tetreault, Expedited Engineering    
Exhibit B: Site Plan; dated 06/25/2025; revised 08/08/2025; revised 08/25/2025; 
revised 09/23/2025; revised 10/10/2025; revised 10/31/2025; revised 
12/10/2025; revised 03/13/2026; revised 04/27/2026; revised 05/26/2026;  
prepared by James L. Tetreault, Expedited Engineering, LLC

10)   Request for Certificate of Compliance 
a. 51 Oriol Drive (CC-2022-065)
Ms. VandenBoom reviewed the request for a Certificate of Compliance for 51 Oriel Drive, a 
large apartment complex previously permitted under a local Wetlands Ordinance filing. 
Staff reported that there are no wetlands associated with the property and that the 
Conservation Commission’s jurisdiction was limited to ensuring compliance with the 
stormwater and erosion control conditions applicable to the original permit. A site visit 
conducted by staff on the preceding Friday confirmed that the site was fully stabilized. An 
as-built plan and a certification letter from the engineer of record were submitted, 
verifying compliance with the approved stormwater design.  
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 by roll call vote to issue the Certificate of Compliance. 
List of Exhibits: 
Exhibit A: Certificate of Compliance Request; dated 03/04/2026; prepared by Mark 
Borenstein, Prince Lobel  
Exhibit B: As-built Plan; dated 06/12/2026; prepared by Andrew J. Ruggles, Allen & 
Major 
b. 2 Lodi Street (fka 50 Lafayette Street) (CC-2023-073 & DEP# 349-1403)  
Ms. VandenBoom reviewed the request and noted the Commission had reviewed this a the 
previous meeting.  She confirmed the requested modification had been made on the fence.  
She confirmed that staff have no concerns about this item moving forward for a Certificate 
of Compliance.  
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 by roll call vote to issue the Certificate of Compliance. 
List of Exhibits: 
Exhibit A: Certificate of Compliance Request; dated 06/04/2026; prepared by Carla 
Pires  
c. 70 Webster Street (CC-2024-033 & DEP#349-1394) 
Nick Kelling, Level Design Group, LLC, on behalf of the applicant, Gold Star Builders, Inc. 
explained that while the project had been largely constructed in accordance with the 
approved plans, several minor modifications were made during construction.  the 
transformer pad had been relocated due to instructions from the electric utility. 
Additionally, the western parking aisle width had been reduced from 24 feet to 22 feet, a 
change permissible under the special permit issued for that portion of the project. Mr. 
Nick further explained that a guardrail previously proposed had instead been replaced 
with a two‑foot‑high concrete-retaining wall topped by a four‑foot aluminum safety fence. 
Although this differed from the approved plan, he confirmed that the wall and fence served 
the same functional purpose as the guardrail and provided equal or better safety 
containment.  He also reported extending riprap by approximately five feet along a section 
of slope to improve erosion control near a concrete retaining wall.
Ms. VandenBoom noted the Commission had previously requested installation of shrubs 
downgradient of the outfall, but the applicant determined that installation would require 
disturbance of well-established vegetation. She agreed that avoiding unnecessary 
disturbance was reasonable.         
 
Upon a motion by Commissioner Nystrom, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 3-0 to issue a certificate of compliance.   
List of Exhibits: 
Exhibit A: Certificate of Compliance Request; dated 06/24/2026; prepared by 
Nicola Facendola, Level Design Group, LLC   
Exhibit B: As-built Plan; dated 06/16/2026; prepared by Nicola Facendola, Level 
Design Group, LLC   
9) Enforcement Order and Violation Updates 
a. 133 Lake Avenue North (CC-2020-007) 
b. 99 Wildwood Avenue (CC-EO-2020-009) 
c. 166 Moreland Street (CC-EO-2020-011) 
d. 269 James Street (CC-EO-2021-007) 
e. 4 Tiffany Avenue (CC-EO-2023-001) 
f. 570 Lincoln Street (CC-EO-2023-010) 
g. 198 Granite Street (CC-EO-2024-001) 
Glenn Krevosky of EBT Environmental Consultants appeared, accompanied by property 
owner representative Mr. Chris Dimarzio. Mr. Krevosky began by addressing the 
Commission’s prior questions concerning the sediment removal plan and clarified 
discrepancies identified between the narrative and the plan sheets. Specifically, he noted 
that one plan sheet referenced 3–4‑inch subangular rock while another referenced 6–
10‑inch rock, and he explained that the latter range—extending up to 10 inches—was the 
correct specification for the largest rock intended for channel stabilization. He further 
clarified that the channel reconstruction would utilize stone ranging from the larger 
10‑inch pieces down to smaller grades to replicate appropriate natural gradation. 
 
Mr. Krevosky described the sedimentation and scour conditions within the channel. He 
noted that a photograph submitted as part of the record demonstrated severe scour below 
the existing culvert, attributable to the increased peak flows created by upstream 
impervious surfaces. He related these findings to NOAA analyses indicating trends of 
higher peak flow events. In support of the proposed remediation methods, Mr. Krevosky 
referenced a previous 260‑foot channel reconstruction project conducted by EBT in 
Oxford, Massachusetts, where subangular rock and engineered grading withstood much 
greater flows from a one‑square‑mile watershed. He emphasized that EBT was 
well‑experienced in designing and reconstructing channels to withstand high‑intensity 
storm events.
He then reviewed the planned method of sediment removal. The work would be completed 
primarily using a mid‑sized John Deere 75G excavator equipped with a cleanup bucket. He 
reiterated that the earlier augering performed by EBT had identified the A‑horizon 
beneath the sediment, confirming that excavation could be performed to a known, stable 
soil layer. Mr. Krevosky emphasized that the excavation would be conducted carefully to 
prevent damage to the underlying mineral layer and to preserve the integrity of the 
wetland system. 
 
Mr. Krevosky next explained the bypass strategy for maintaining flow during excavation. 
An 8‑inch bypass pipe would be used to divert water from the culvert to a stable channel. 
He stated that during recent high‑flow events—specifically during the storm that 
contributed to peak flows into the Blackstone River—he observed that water flowing from 
the Granite Street culvert had been effectively captured by National Grid’s newly installed 
crushed‑stone driveway and supplemental subsurface drainage trench. These structures 
had prevented high flows from entering the sediment removal area, and Mr. Krevosky 
expressed confidence that similar capacity would prevent stormwater from interfering 
with the sediment removal during construction. 
He then described the restoration plan, noting that existing elderberry and arrowwood 
shrubs located in the upper wet meadow would be salvaged and replanted. Additional 
upland and wetland plantings would be installed post‑excavation, although he stated that 
hydric soils were not expected to remain once sediment was removed down to the 
A‑horizon. This would allow planting of species appropriate to the underlying mineral 
substrate. 
 
At this point, Mr. Dimarzio addressed the Commission regarding the disposition of the 
excavated sediment. He explained that negotiations were ongoing with National Grid, the 
underlying landowner of the adjacent transmission corridor. While initial discussions with 
National Grid suggested that the material could remain onsite or be relocated to another 
portion of National Grid property, updated internal guidance from the utility appeared to 
require disposal at a remote location. This would impose significant trucking and handling 
costs on the applicant. Mr. Dimarzio reported that he had spoken with National Grid 
representatives that morning and believed that internal discussions were continuing. He 
stated that the applicant had offered to indemnify National Grid to allow the sediment to 
be transported and stockpiled on a portion of land owned by the applicant beneath the 
transmission lines. He added that, at minimum, the applicant hoped National Grid would 
allow temporary stockpiling so that removal could proceed during the dry season, even if 
final disposal arrangements were not yet resolved.
The Commission and staff then discussed the remaining procedural requirements for 
authorizing the sediment removal work. Mr. Flint emphasized that because the property is 
subject to a conservation restriction held jointly by Greater Worcester Land Trust and 
Mass Audubon, the Commission must receive written confirmation from those 
organizations that the proposed work is permissible under the terms of the restriction. He 
also reported that the City Law Department was drafting a license agreement that would 
allow access to the city‑owned portion of the site for excavation. Once the Commission 
received approvals from the conservation restriction holders and once the license 
agreement was in place, the Commission could formally amend the enforcement order to 
require implementation of the sediment removal plan.  
 
Mr. Dimarzio anticipated having an update from National Grid by the Commission’s next 
meeting on August 3.  Mr. Flint stated that written responses from Mass Audubon and 
Greater Worcester Land Trust should also be received by the next meeting and that the 
license agreement should be ready at that time. Accordingly, staff indicated that the 
Commission would be in a position at the August 3 meeting to consider formally amending 
the Enforcement Order to authorize the work.

15) Commission Liaison Update
Lake Quinsigamond Commission
Ms. VandenBoom reported that the primary topic at that meeting was the growing use of  
wake boats on the lake. Several individuals addressed the Lake Commission both in favor of 
and in opposition to wake boats. Concerns raised included shoreline erosion caused by the 
large wakes generated by these boats, safety considerations for swimmers and other  
boaters, and environmental implications such as the potential spread of invasive aquatic  
species through ballast water intake and discharge. She noted that the Lake Commission 
had not made any regulatory decisions at that meeting but continued to explore options,  
including restrictions based on distance from shore or water depth. The matter remained  
under active discussion.
